title: DePIN on Solana: Shaga's Gamer-Owned Cloud Gaming Network with Co-Founder Daeshawn Ballard
description:
Gaming used to start in arcades, where you saved your allowance to drop quarters into a slot. Then it moved to the living room. Then online, with friends all over the world. Daeshawn Ballard, co-founder and COO of Shaga, wants to give the quarters back to the gamers.

Cloud gaming companies spend hundreds of millions, sometimes billions, building data centers. But not everyone lives close enough to one for it to feel responsive. Latency kills the moment you press the button expecting an advantage. Shaga's answer is to skip the mega data center entirely.

Shaga turns idle gaming PCs into mini data centers and connects them into a network on Solana. A gamer can pull compute from a node across the street instead of one across the country. The owner of that PC, the node operator, earns from the gameplay running on their hardware. As Daeshawn puts it, they become an arcade owner.

The result is cloud gaming infrastructure that reaches more people, runs on lower latency, and shares the upside with the gamers building it.

"We're democratizing who gets the access, and also who gets to share in the economic upside of the gaming infrastructure."

Learn more at shaga.xyz

asr.full_text: Where did gaming start? Arcades You had to save up your allowance money to put those quarters in a slot then it evolved and you can play at home and then now you can play at home with your friends all over the world At Cheyga, you've become the owner of the distribution network so instead of it going directly to that company those quarters are mainly going to gamers like you and I I've been a gamer my entire life. It's how we bonded as a family, with my friends. Gaming brought my co-founder and I together. We had this goal of, man, I really wanted a gaming PC in college, but I couldn't afford it. What if I could just have a PC? And when I was in class, it's being able to pay for itself. And then when I come back with the games that I wanna PC. And when I was in class, being able to pay for itself and then when I come back, I play that game that I want to play. And that idea from university never left him. As video games tried their hand at multiplayer experiences, companies wanted to start scaling but not everybody lives in an optimal range to a lot of these data centers. People are like, Hey, what's going on? I can't access it you know it's not working, that latency issue that press this button because I think I have the advantage I need that reaction to happen at that particular moment. If not I'm screwed you got me kill streak done. So in order to get rid of that lag what we've been able to do is make a bunch of mini data centers by turning gaming PC's into these mini data centers. So now a gamer can access this compute that they otherwise would get from a data center that's miles away to maybe somebody who's right across the street who knows. Our vision is that all these cloud gaming companies that are spending hundreds of millions and even billions of dollars on these data centers that still don't reach every gamer out there, redirecting those investment dollars who use the rails that are powered by people, we're democratizing who gets the access then also who gets to share in the economic upside of the gaming infrastructure. If you set up a node, you're essentially an arcade owner. You're inviting people to come in with their quarters to play your games and you're getting the economic upside from it. On the other side, as a gamer, I can just use my phone and hop right into the arcade.
